hero.headline: Free mammogram screenings offered in Jupiter and West Palm Beach next month
hero.teaser: Promise Fund will hold free Mammography Screening Days on July 11 in Jupiter and July 12 in West Palm Beach for women who are uninsured, underinsured or have limited access to health care.
hero.body:
Women in Palm Beach County can access free mammogram screenings at two upcoming events hosted by Promise Fund, a South Florida nonprofit dedicated to improving breast and cervical cancer survivorship. The organization will hold screening days on July 11 in Jupiter and July 12 in West Palm Beach. These events are made possible through partnerships with Florida Mobile Mammography, HealthyMe, the Health Care District of Palm Beach County, Origin Church, the Florida Department of Health and Monarch Health Services.

The first screening event takes place July 11 starting at 8 a.m. at a location on Indiantown Road in Jupiter. The second event is scheduled for July 12 beginning at 9 a.m. in West Palm Beach. Appointments are required to participate in either event. Women interested in attending can register by calling 877-427-7664.

Lissette Lahoz, Promise Fund's Palm Beach County navigator, emphasized the importance of these free screening opportunities. She stated, "The Promise Fund is here to make screenings accessible for everyone, especially those who might otherwise go without care." Lahoz added that early detection can significantly impact treatment outcomes, saying, "Early detection can make a real difference. Treatment is often easier to manage, and people are able to focus more on their health, their families, and their everyday lives."

Promise Fund serves uninsured, underinsured, and underserved women throughout Palm Beach, Broward and Martin counties. The organization has reached more than 145,000 women across South Florida through education and advocacy efforts. To date, more than 27,000 women have accessed screenings, diagnostics and care through Promise Fund's programs, and the nonprofit has provided assistance to 286 women diagnosed with cancer as they navigate treatment. Promise Fund currently operates four co-located screening programs in Palm Beach and Broward counties and is working to establish a similar program in Martin County.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach woman posed as parking official in Worth Avenue scam, Palm Beach police say
cards.body:
A 19-year-old West Palm Beach resident has been arrested after allegedly impersonating a parking official and defrauding visitors on Worth Avenue. According to Palm Beach police, Ti'Miyah De'Asia Allen posed as a representative of both ParkMobile and the Palm Beach Parking Authority while conducting an illegal scheme targeting drivers in the area.

The scam worked by offering unsuspecting victims a discounted parking rate. Allen would approach people either before they paid for parking or while they were in the process of paying. She would tell them they could pay her approximately $1 instead of the legitimate rate of $5 per hour plus a 40-cent transaction fee. To appear credible, Allen carried what looked like a ParkMobile payment device and displayed a fake badge. According to police, the victims targeted in these encounters were predominantly over 65 years old. When victims provided their credit card information, fraudulent charges appeared on their accounts. In at least one case documented in an arrest affidavit from June 5, a victim experienced a $2,500 unauthorized charge to a company called Health Aid.

Beyond the direct harm to individual victims, police say the scheme also deprived the town of legitimate parking revenue that should have been collected through proper channels. The fraudulent transactions represent money that would otherwise have gone to the municipality's parking fund.

This is not Allen's first brush with law enforcement involving financial schemes. Police say she was involved in a similar operation last year while employed at a Wawa location on Belvedere Road. During that incident, she allegedly voided customer transactions for personal profit. Allen now faces three charges related to the Worth Avenue scheme: falsely impersonating an officer, organized scheme to defraud, and unlawful use of a badge or other indicia of authority. The combination of charges reflects the deliberate nature of her deception and the coordinated effort to present herself as an official authority figure while stealing from vulnerable residents and visitors.

cards.headline: $1 million federal grant funds Ixora Park sewage system upgrade in Indian River County
cards.teaser: A $1 million federal grant will help fund a $20.8 million project to retrofit the sewage system in the Ixora Park community in Indian River County, affecting ov.
cards.body:
A $1 million federal grant will help fund a $20.8 million project to retrofit the sewage system in the Ixora Park community in Indian River County, Congressman Mike Haridopolos announced at a Wednesday afternoon press conference. The Member Community Project Funding will address the needs of over 230 homes that currently rely on a failing sewer system risking contamination of environmental resources. The community sits adjacent to the County South Relief Canal, which discharges into the Indian River Lagoon, one of the most diverse estuaries in the country.

The project will replace aging sewer infrastructure and is designed to protect water quality by reducing discharges of nitrogen and phosphorus into the lagoon. Haridopolos said federal support ensures health and safety to the community while protecting the Indian River Lagoon, a designated federal resource. Keith Drewett of the Clean Water Coalition of Indian River County noted the upgrade is critical because of the area's environmental conditions and high water table. Haridopolos added that the benefits extend beyond environmental protection, as replacing the aging infrastructure improves both water quality and the taxable value of homes in the community.

cards.headline: All detainees transferred from Everglades immigration facility as hurricane season begins
cards.teaser: U.S.
cards.body:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has transferred all detainees from the Everglades detention facility known as "Alligator Alcatraz" as Florida enters hurricane season, according to an ICE spokesperson. The soft-sided facility, built near Big Cypress National Preserve and opened in July 2024, became the center of political, legal and environmental disputes. An ICE spokesperson stated the transfers were made "for the safety of the illegal alien detainees." The New York Times reported that concerns about conditions, detainee treatment and costs prompted the Department of Homeland Security to wind down the site. The project has drawn scrutiny over spending, with critics saying the state spent at least half a billion dollars tied to the effort. Gov. Ron DeSantis defended the facility as a temporary tool that helped process and deport migrants, saying it "saved lives" and "relieved burdens on taxpayers," though he did not confirm operations had fully stopped.

Environmental groups and Democrats continue challenging the facility. Friends of the Everglades and the Center for Biological Diversity sued to stop activity, arguing the state and federal governments failed to follow environmental laws before building in an ecologically sensitive area. Eve Samples, executive director of Friends of the Everglades, called for "remediation of that harm and a return to the lightly used training runway that existed before June of last year." House Minority Leader Fentrice Driskell questioned whether the half-billion dollars should have been allocated to affordable housing or teacher pay. The state continues seeking federal reimbursement, with FEMA releasing only a small portion of the $58 million requested.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Teen Killed in Shooting After Instagram Gun Exchange
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce teenager was killed in a shooting that followed a planned firearm exchange arranged through Instagram.
cards.body:
A teenager in Fort Pierce was fatally shot during what police say was a planned gun exchange arranged through Instagram. The shooting occurred while the victim was riding a bicycle, marking what authorities described as an unusual incident for the area. According to Fort Pierce police, the exchange of firearms through social media leading to the fatal shooting represents a notable development in local crime patterns.

The incident has drawn attention from law enforcement as an example of how social media platforms can facilitate dangerous transactions. Police characterized the Instagram-arranged gun deal as a first of its kind in their jurisdiction, highlighting the evolving nature of criminal activity in the community. The victim, identified in available records as Maria Jesus Barajas Aguilar, was engaged in the bicycle when the shooting took place.

Investigators have been working to piece together the events that led to the deadly confrontation. Fort Pierce police continue their investigation into the circumstances surrounding the shooting, including details about who arranged the exchange and the individuals involved in the transaction. Authorities are examining how the social media platform was used to coordinate the meeting that ultimately turned fatal.

The case underscores concerns about the risks associated with arranging firearm transactions through social media channels. Police have not yet announced any arrests in connection with the shooting, and the investigation remains ongoing as detectives work to identify suspects and determine exactly what transpired during the exchange. The incident has prompted continued scrutiny of how dangerous transactions occur within local communities and the role digital platforms play in facilitating them.

cards.headline: Planned Gun Exchange Led to Fatal Fort Pierce Bike Shooting
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police said a planned gun exchange resulted in a shooting that killed a teenager on a bicycle.
cards.body:
A teenager was killed in a Fort Pierce shooting that stemmed from a planned firearm exchange, according to police. The victim was on a bicycle when the shooting occurred.

Investigators determined the shooting was connected to an arrangement to exchange guns. The planned exchange ended in gunfire that claimed the teen's life.

Fort Pierce police continue to investigate the circumstances of the shooting. Detectives are working to identify all individuals involved in the planned gun transaction that turned deadly.

cards.headline: Indian River County sewage system getting $1 million federal grant for Ixora Park upgrade
cards.teaser: A $1 million federal grant will help fund a major sewage system upgrade in Indian River County, Congressman Mike Haridopolos announced at a press conference Wed.
cards.body:
A $1 million federal grant will help fund a major sewage system upgrade in Indian River County, Congressman Mike Haridopolos announced at an afternoon press conference Wednesday. The Member Community Project Funding will go toward a $20.8 million project to retrofit the sewage system in the Ixora Park community, affecting over 230 homes that currently rely on a failing sewer system that risks contaminating environmental resources. The community sits adjacent to the County South Relief Canal, which discharges into the Indian River Lagoon, one of the most diverse estuaries in the country.

Haridopolos said federal support for the project ensures health and safety to the community by rehabilitating infrastructure for over 230 homes while protecting a designated federal resource, the Indian River Lagoon. The project will replace aging sewer infrastructure and is designed to protect water quality by reducing discharges of nitrogen and phosphorus into the lagoon. Keith Drewett of the Clean Water Coalition of Indian River County noted that the upgrade is critical because of the area's environmental conditions, stating "The water table is so high, there's so much rain that's all just flowing underground through the subsurface." Haridopolos said the benefits extend beyond environmental protection, noting that replacing the aging infrastructure improves not only water quality but also the taxable value of homes.

cards.headline: Jupiter beach dance parties to continue at sea turtle nesting area with new lighting rules
cards.teaser: Weekend beach dance parties will continue at Jupiter's sea turtle nesting area with lighting adjustments. The Town of Jupiter convened a meeting Wednesday afternoon bringing together local, county, and state stakeholders.
cards.body:
The Town of Jupiter held a meeting Wednesday afternoon at the police department to address concerns about weekend beach dance parties held in a sea turtle nesting area. Local, county, and state stakeholders attended along with representatives from Loggerhead Marinelife Center. The meeting lasted about an hour and a half. Following the gathering, representatives from the dance group said it was productive and that the parties will continue with adjustments. "We're going to continue, just a couple of adjustments. Beautiful," said Foreli of Happy Beach Dancing.

The adjustments will focus on reducing lighting during events to avoid disturbing nesting sea turtles. Some had called for moving the dancing away from the area entirely during nesting season. The group said they will return to Beach Access 55 this Saturday.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County public safety spending becomes focus of property tax debate
cards.teaser: When Palm Beach County Administrator Joe Abruzzo confronted the state's Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia about cutting property taxes, the issue of spending on public safety was a main point of contention.
cards.body:
When Palm Beach County Administrator Joe Abruzzo confronted state Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia about cutting property taxes, public safety spending emerged as a central point of disagreement. According to Abruzzo, most taxpayer dollars collected in the county fund public safety, with $1.1 billion allocated to the sheriff and approximately $700 million to fire rescue. "If you add up all our departments there is only $609 million when you remove the first responders, and the $609 million is what he is essentially attacking and I'm trying to explain to him how it works," Abruzzo said Tuesday.

Ingoglia came to Boca Raton this week to announce Palm Beach County was overspending by $443 million and to make the case for a referendum this fall that would raise the Homestead Exemption to $250,000 in 2027 and $500,000 in 2028. Abruzzo met Ingoglia at the news conference to invite him to review the county's budget. Abruzzo noted that approximately $73 million in new revenue this year is already being absorbed by the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, which is requesting a $94 million increase. In a statement, PBSO said ensuring citizen safety and security remains a funding priority.

cards.headline: Lake Worth Beach commission approves 10-year lease extension for Benny's on the Beach
cards.teaser: The Lake Worth Beach City Commission unanimously approved a 10-year lease extension for Benny's on the Beach, pushing the pier restaurant's lease from January 2033 to February 2043 with a 5% rent increase every two years.
cards.body:
The Lake Worth Beach City Commission unanimously approved a 10-year lease extension for Benny's on the Beach, extending the pier restaurant's lease from January 2033 to February 2043 with a 5% rent increase every two years. The decision followed public debate over fairness, community benefit, and the timing of the extension, which comes seven years before the current agreement expires. Dylan Lipton, the restaurant's owner, defended the extension by highlighting Benny's four decades in the community and its status as a year-round anchor supporting surrounding businesses. Lipton noted the restaurant employs more than 100 local residents, invests $1 million annually in maintenance, repairs, utilities, and improvements, and serves as a major tourism driver.

Opposition emerged from several residents. Jenny Powell questioned the timing and benefits to residents, while Kim Stokes raised concerns about unequal treatment compared to the commission's recent discussions about the Beach Club. Nancy Udell warned against limiting future commissions' options. Commissioner Christopher Serafinchan led advocacy for the extension, calling Benny's the city's highest-paying tenant. Commissioners Sarah Malega and Mimi May supported the extension, with May citing the restaurant's ongoing property investment and community role. Mayor Betty Resch framed it as providing stability for the long-standing business.

cards.headline: Jupiter surgeon uses opioid-free recovery protocol to prevent addiction before it starts
cards.teaser: Andrew Noble, an orthopedic surgeon at Jupiter Medical Center, uses the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery protocol combined with his own proprietary method to help patients recover from joint replacement surgery without opioids.
cards.body:
Andrew Noble, an orthopedic surgeon at Jupiter Medical Center, is using the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocol combined with his own proprietary method to help patients recover from joint replacement surgery without opioids. The ERAS protocol combines robotics for minimally invasive surgery, targeted numbing, and a timed schedule of non-opioid medications taken before, during, and after surgery. "Instead of chasing pain, it's a way of trying to stay ahead of pain, and have less pain afterwards with less need for opioids," Noble said.

Patient April Stubbs recovered from knee replacement surgery without opioids using this approach. "I never had to touch the more serious pain medications. The opioids never even had to take any," Stubbs said. Daniel Warren, Chief Marketing Officer at Reprieve Recovery in Jupiter, emphasized that patients often don't understand the physical effects of opioid medications during surgical recovery. "They'll take a substance for two weeks, and they'll feel uncomfortable, or they'll go through withdrawals, and they don't even know why, like they were never educated that you can withdraw from those medications," Warren said. Noble said the goal is to "get patients through a surgery, better pain control, and having them with a quick recovery and satisfied results without the opioid exposure."

cards.headline: Jupiter approves fire assessment fee to fund new fire rescue department launching October 1
cards.teaser: Jupiter town council approved a fire assessment fee to help fund the town's new fire rescue department, which begins service Oct. 1. The fee will cover about 8% of the total cost of the department.
cards.body:
Jupiter's town council has approved a fire assessment fee to fund the town's new fire rescue department, which begins service Oct. 1. The per-property charge will cover about 8% of the total cost of the department, with property taxes funding 84% and EMS transport fees covering the remaining 8%. The assessment will replace the current county fire fee that appears on residents' tax bills. Finance Director Scott Reynolds said the move represents significant savings for property owners, citing immediate savings of $10 million to residents.

Mayor Jim Kuretski was the lone no vote on the funding structure, raising concerns about how the assessment is calculated across different property types. Single family homes are being assessed based on total square footage including garages and porches, while townhomes and condos are not. The town sent letters to 30,000 homes explaining the fee. Town of Jupiter spokesperson Mariana DiNunzio acknowledged the change has caused confusion because the town has not had to implement a non ad-valorem assessment before. The town has established an online calculator where residents can see their potential savings.

cards.headline: Martin County residents push for public access to Martin County High School pool
cards.teaser: Residents packed a Martin County joint commission meeting on Tuesday, calling on local leaders to open the pool at Martin County High School to the public as an affordable resource for swim education.
cards.body:
Residents packed a Martin County joint commission meeting on Tuesday, calling on local leaders to open the pool at Martin County High School to the public as an affordable resource for swim education. The nonprofit Martin Swims asked local leaders to put a referendum on the November ballot that would create a fund to establish community pools. They suggested residents pay less than $10 a year per property to fund the pool on the Martin County High School campus. Ricki Stein, a Martin County resident, said free access is key to getting children comfortable in the water because kids learn through play. Dick Landrum, another Martin County resident, said Martin County has several venues that teach people how to swim but most of them are costly. He said the group wants it to be a community service.

Both county and school district leaders expressed a level of support for the idea. Martin County Commissioner Ed Ciampi recognized that if you teach a child to swim, then they're an adult that also knows how to swim. Martin County School District Superintendent Michael Maine said he is already making plans to set up a meeting with Martin Swims to explore the logistics. Dr. Blanche Wells, president of Martin Swims, said the cause is personal and urgent and that it's life-saving.

cards.headline: Two out of three Floridians say higher gas prices could tank summer road trips
cards.teaser: A new survey shows two out of three Floridians says higher prices could tank their summer road trips this year, even as gas prices are starting to fall.
cards.body:
A new survey by RV Windshield Replacement shows two out of three Floridians say higher gas prices could "tank" their summer road trips this year. The company conducted the survey to gauge how costs are reshaping vacation plans. Florida drivers polled say if gas prices go up another $1.01, their summer road trip travel would be off. One driver at a gas station on 45th Street in West Palm Beach told WPTV there is no way they could afford it, saying "no one can unless you're rich."

The survey found 68% of Florida drivers agree shorter state trips might be most doable, but some say even that could be tough to pull off. A WPTV viewer said that for trips to Orlando, instead of going every two weeks, they now go about once a month or sometimes skip a month entirely because of gas prices. Gas prices have started to fall just as the survey results emerged.

cards.headline: Portugal fans in Palm Beach County pack Loxahatchee club for World Cup opening match
cards.teaser: Dozens of Portugal supporters packed the Portuguese American Culture Society of Palm Beach County in Loxahatchee on Wednesday to watch the team's first match of.
cards.body:
Dozens of Portugal supporters packed the Portuguese American Culture Society of Palm Beach County in Loxahatchee to watch the team's first World Cup match, surrounded by Portuguese beer, wine, and food from the Iberian Peninsula. Vic Piorro, treasurer of the club, said the energy in the room reflected how deeply soccer is woven into Portuguese identity. The club has served as a gathering place for the local Portuguese community since 1981, starting as a place to gather, speak the language, eat traditional food, and observe Portuguese traditions and culture.

Among the fans in attendance were Jonathan Reinoso and his father, Johnny-Lee Reinoso, who left work early to make it to the club in time for kickoff. Jonathan has been a superfan since childhood. When the Portuguese national team set down roots in Palm Beach Gardens for their practice facility, his father got his son a chance to meet the team, including Cristiano Ronaldo. Jonathan said meeting Ronaldo was a dream and he was in complete shock. Even though the game ended in a tie, the night was still a celebration for the Reinoso family and everyone else at the club. For Jonathan, being in that room with fellow fans is something that goes beyond the scoreboard.

cards.headline: Indian River County sewage system in Ixora Park gets $1 million federal grant
cards.teaser: The federal funding will help pay for a $20.8 million project to retrofit the sewage system in the Ixora Park community, affecting over 230 homes that currently rely on a failing sewer system.
cards.body:
A $1 million federal grant will help fund a major sewage system upgrade in Indian River County, Congressman Mike Haridopolos announced at an afternoon press conference Wednesday. The Member Community Project Funding will go toward a $20.8 million project to retrofit the sewage system in the Ixora Park community, affecting over 230 homes that currently rely on a failing sewer system that risks contaminating environmental resources. Haridopolos said the federal support ensures health and safety to the community by rehabilitating infrastructure while protecting the Indian River Lagoon, a designated federal resource.

The community sits adjacent to the County South Relief Canal, which discharges into the Indian River Lagoon, one of the most diverse estuaries in the country. Keith Drewett of the Clean Water Coalition of Indian River County noted the lagoon has changed dramatically over the past twenty years, with fewer people swimming in it. The Clean Water Coalition says the upgrade is critical because of the area's environmental conditions, with high water tables and heavy rain flowing underground through the subsurface. The project will replace aging sewer infrastructure and reduce discharges of nitrogen and phosphorus into the lagoon while also improving the taxable value of homes in the area.

cards.headline: Jupiter approves fire assessment fee for new fire rescue department starting Oct. 1
cards.teaser: Jupiter's town council approved a fire assessment fee to help fund the town's new fire rescue department, which begins service Oct. 1. The fee will cover about 8% of the total cost of the department.
cards.body:
Jupiter's town council has approved a fire assessment fee to fund the town's new fire rescue department, which begins service Oct. 1. The per-property charge will cover about 8% of the total cost of the department. Property taxes will fund 84% of the department, with the remaining 8% collected through EMS transport fees. The assessment will replace the current county fire fee that appears on residents' tax bills.

Finance Director Scott Reynolds said the move represents significant savings for property owners, citing a $10 million savings compared to initial projections from three years ago. Mayor Jim Kuretski was the lone no vote on the funding structure, raising concerns about how the assessment is calculated across different property types. Single family homes are being assessed based on total square footage including garages and porches, while townhomes and condos are not. The town sent letters to 30,000 homes explaining the fee and has established an online calculator where residents can see their potential savings. Town of Jupiter spokesperson Mariana DiNunzio acknowledged the change has caused some confusion because it is new and the town has not had a non ad-valorem assessment before.

cards.headline: Prosecutors to subpoena Tiger Woods medical records in Jupiter Island DUI case
cards.teaser: Florida prosecutors will issue a subpoena for Tiger Woods' medical records after he pleaded not guilty to driving under the influence following an arrest in March on Jupiter Island.
cards.body:
Florida prosecutors will issue a subpoena for Tiger Woods' medical records following his not guilty plea to driving under the influence after an arrest in March on Jupiter Island. The State of Florida filed a notice on June 15 in the County Court of the Nineteenth Judicial Circuit in Martin County, announcing the subpoena will be issued on June 30 for records related to Woods' treatment or hospitalization.

The subpoena will specifically seek any and all reports documenting statements Woods made regarding alcohol or chemical substance use, any and all drug screen results, and the name of the person who performed any testing. The filing was submitted by Assistant State Attorney Nirlaine Tallandier Smartt on behalf of State Attorney Thomas R. Any objections to the subpoena must be delivered to the Assistant State Attorney within 10 days.

cards.headline: Two out of three Florida drivers say higher gas prices could tank summer road trips
cards.teaser: Florida drivers polled say if gas prices go up another $1.01, their summer road trip travel is off. Gas prices are starting to fall just in time for summer travel season.
cards.body:
A new survey by RV Windshield Replacement reveals that two out of three Floridians say higher gas prices could "tank" their summer road trips this year. The survey found that Florida drivers polled say if gas prices increase another $1.01, their summer road trip travel plans would be cancelled. WPTV Anchor Hollani Davis spoke with drivers at a gas station on 45th Street in West Palm Beach about whether they could afford summer travel. "There is no way," one driver told Davis. "No one can unless you're rich," said another driver WPTV connected with.

The survey shows 68% of Florida drivers agree that shorter state trips might be the most doable option, but some say even that could be difficult to manage. One WPTV viewer said that for trips to Orlando, they have had to adjust their travel frequency because of gas prices. Instead of going every two weeks, they now go about once a month, or sometimes skip a month altogether due to fuel costs.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County Library summer reading challenge runs through July 31
hero.teaser: The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to participate in its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, running through July 31 with free activities, incentives and grand prizes.
hero.body:
Community Engagement Manager Lindsey McMullen told WPTV the program offers free activities, incentives and grand prizes to encourage residents to rediscover the joy of reading. Participants can register at any library branch, complete an activity log and return it to claim a prize while supplies last. McMullen said returned logs will also qualify readers for a drawing to win one of several grand prizes.

Little learners up to age 4 can take home a fun rubber duck. Kids ages 5 to 11 can choose from a fidget spinner, dinosaur-themed pop keychain or dino pencil. Teens ages 12 to 17 and adults can opt for a fidget spinner, chip clip or notebook. In addition to the reading challenge, each branch is hosting special events from children's story times and craft sessions to adult workshops and wellness programs.

McMullen added that families will also see Dewey the Library Owl and Penelope Rex, a dinosaur character visiting for the challenge, at various appearances. Summertime reading programs help prevent the summer slide in student learning, according to the American Library Association. Logs can be picked up and turned in on-site. The challenge is open to all county residents and library cardholders.

cards.headline: Rapids Water Park hosts adults night, free dad admission and safety event in Riviera Beach
cards.teaser: Rapids Water Park is hosting special summer events including adults-only nights, free admission for dads during Father's Day weekend, and participation in the World's Largest Swim Lesson on June 25.
cards.body:
Rapids Water Park is hosting several special events this summer for guests of all ages. Elliott Russell, director of marketing and sales, told WPTV that Adults Night returns with music, glow items, and exclusive park access for guests 21 and older. The event gives grown-ups a chance to enjoy the slides, lazy river, and wave pool under the stars. Greg Fuller, the park's general manager, said families can also take advantage of free admission for dads on June 20-21 during Father's Day weekend.

On June 25, Rapids will join Live Like Jake and other participants worldwide for the World's Largest Swim Lesson, a coordinated effort to raise awareness about water safety. The park, located at 6566 N. Military Trail in Riviera Beach, is open daily with various ticket packages. New offerings this season include specialty funnel cakes and other viral treats.

cards.headline: Smithsonian Marine Exhibit in Fort Pierce offers close-up look at Florida coastal ecosystems
cards.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to explore Florida's coastal habitats through live, complex ecosystem displays in Fort Pierce's waterfront district. According to Manager Bill Hoffman, this approach to exhibiting fully functional marine environments has been the facility's cornerstone since 1980, distinguishing it from most other public aquariums. "We feel like we're the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast, and we don't want to be," Hoffman said, noting that the facility houses more species than many larger exhibits. The centerpiece is the Atlantic coral reef tank, which recreates one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Beyond the coral display, visitors encounter live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities that showcase intricate relationships between organisms, including a four-inch barracuda.

The touch tank, managed by exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran, remains a popular attraction where guests can handle unusual marine species under staff supervision and encounter animals they've likely never seen before. The exhibit operates through a partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station to educate the public about ocean conservation and threats facing marine environments. Hoffman emphasized that healthy ecosystems depend on countless small organisms, a lesson reinforced through the facility's living displays. The facility is planning special programming as part of its 25th anniversary celebration later this year. Located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce, the facility welcomes visitors year-round. More information is available at sms.si.edu and on the Smithsonian Marine Station's social media channels.

hero.headline: Attorney General Ashley Moody and Senator Rick Scott secure nearly $1 billion for Florida military installations
hero.teaser: The funding, provided through the Senate National Defense Authorization Act, will support military personnel, installations and defense industrial bases throughout Florida.
hero.body:
Attorney General Ashley Moody and Senator Rick Scott have announced that Florida will receive nearly $1 billion in federal funding for military installations across the state. The $935 million allocation comes through the Senate National Defense Authorization Act, which was approved this year. The funding will support military personnel, installations, and defense industrial bases throughout Florida. Once President Donald Trump signs the legislation, the money will be implemented in the federal 2027 fiscal year budget.

Moody emphasized the personal significance of the funding to her as a member of a military family. "Supporting our armed forces is not just my job — as a mom in a military family, it is personal to me. These wins are not just allocated dollars; they are a down payment on the future of our military in Florida, aimed at strengthening the state's installations and defense industrial base," she said. Serving on the Senate Armed Services Committee, Moody stated that she has worked to ensure military readiness and support from day one. Scott highlighted Florida's strategic military importance, noting that the state hosts more than 20 military installations and three combatant commands. "I am pleased to see so many critical provisions have been included in this year's version of the bill that will help Florida, our warfighters, and our national security," Scott said.

The funding will support numerous critical projects across Florida's military infrastructure. Cape Canaveral Space Force Station will receive support for the Eastern Range, the nation's busiest launch site, including a new command facility, base support and communications warehouses, security forces, vehicle maintenance facilities, and a missile defense test facility. Tyndall Air Force Base in Panama City will receive funding for gate projects and a fire and crash rescue station. Eglin Air Force Base in Fort Walton Beach will get funding to enhance recruit training capacity and design funding for a hangar and physical fitness complex. Homestead Air Force Reserve Base in South Florida will receive a climate-controlled tactical storage warehouse.

Additional projects include upgrades to First Coast military installations. Naval Air Station Jacksonville will add a power generation grid, while Camp Blanding's Florida National Guard installation will add a multipurpose training range. The Marine Corps Support Facility on Blount Island will modernize its communications infrastructure. Naval Air Station Key West will receive funding to construct a command and control facility.

cards.headline: Hillsborough County faces $343 million budget impact from property tax reform proposal
cards.teaser: County officials warn that a property tax overhaul headed to the November ballot could force cuts to public safety, libraries and other services.
cards.body:
Hillsborough County could face a $213 million hit to its countywide general fund and another $130 million squeeze in its unincorporated area fund if voters approve a proposed property tax overhaul in the November 2026 General Election. Budget Director Tom Fesler warned County Commissioners on Wednesday that the proposal would create a $150,000 homestead exemption in Fiscal Year 2027, affecting Hillsborough's Fiscal Year 2028 budget, before increasing to $250,000 the following year. The proposal would also reduce the assessment cap on non-homesteaded properties from 10 percent to 5 percent and require five years of Florida residency to qualify for the expanded exemption. Fesler said about 66 percent of the countywide general fund already goes toward constitutional officers, outside agencies and fire rescue, including the Sheriff. If the proposal passes, ad valorem revenue would no longer cover those services entirely, likely forcing the county to look to alternate revenues.

The library district, which funds Hillsborough's public library system, would see an estimated $21 million impact from the proposed changes. Fesler said the loss in funding would likely affect future library projects, as ad valorem revenues have historically been used to replace and build new libraries. County staff outlined possible options including using reserves, freezing compensation or hiring, reducing nonprofit funding, creating special assessment districts, cutting service hours, raising fees or finding new revenue sources. One possibility would be a public service tax on utility bills, which Fesler estimated could generate about $80 million to $90 million if levied at 10 percent. The constitutional amendment would require 60 percent voter approval.

cards.headline: All detainees transferred from Everglades immigration facility as hurricane season begins
cards.teaser: U.S.
cards.body:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has transferred all detainees from the Everglades detention facility known as "Alligator Alcatraz" as Florida enters hurricane season, according to an ICE spokesperson. The soft-sided facility, built near Big Cypress National Preserve and opened in July 2024, became the center of political, legal and environmental disputes. An ICE spokesperson stated the transfers were made "for the safety of the illegal alien detainees." The New York Times reported that concerns about conditions, detainee treatment and costs prompted the Department of Homeland Security to wind down the site. The project has drawn scrutiny over spending, with critics saying the state spent at least half a billion dollars tied to the effort. Gov. Ron DeSantis defended the facility as a temporary tool that helped process and deport migrants, saying it "saved lives" and "relieved burdens on taxpayers," though he did not confirm operations had fully stopped.

Environmental groups and Democrats continue challenging the facility. Friends of the Everglades and the Center for Biological Diversity sued to stop activity, arguing the state and federal governments failed to follow environmental laws before building in an ecologically sensitive area. Eve Samples, executive director of Friends of the Everglades, called for "remediation of that harm and a return to the lightly used training runway that existed before June of last year." House Minority Leader Fentrice Driskell questioned whether the half-billion dollars should have been allocated to affordable housing or teacher pay. The state continues seeking federal reimbursement, with FEMA releasing only a small portion of the $58 million requested.

cards.headline: Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders proposes 50 percent tax on AI companies to fund sovereign wealth fund
cards.teaser: The proposed legislation would create a nearly $7 trillion fund through a one-time tax on the largest AI companies, with implications for Florida-based tech operations.
cards.body:
U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders has introduced legislation to create a sovereign wealth fund financed through a one-time 50 percent tax on the stock of the largest AI companies. The proposal would apply to AI companies that reach $200 million in annual AI sales, and Sanders estimates the tax would create a nearly $7 trillion fund generating hundreds of billions of dollars annually in direct payments to Americans and programs such as health care, education and housing. Rather than requiring companies to pay cash, the proposal would require them to transfer stock, making the American public a major shareholder in the country's largest AI firms.

A seven-person independent commission, nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate, would manage the fund and use its voting shares to block decisions that hurt the American people and push for policies that help them. Sanders proposes that a 5 percent annual dividend from the fund would provide direct payments of more than $1,000 to every American. The proposal has drawn interest from other figures, including President Donald Trump and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, though Sanders' push is more aggressive. According to those in the room, Sanders and Altman remained far apart on how large of a stake the public would get during their meeting.

cards.headline: Florida Attorney General affirms parental rights over religious instruction in schools
cards.teaser: Attorney General James Uthmeier issued an opinion stating that public schools must respect and accommodate parental decisions about religious instruction.
cards.body:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier issued an opinion reaffirming that parents, not government, bear the primary responsibility for directing the education and religious upbringing of their children. The opinion addressed release time religious instruction programs in response to a question raised by Senator Clay Yarborough. Uthmeier concluded that when parents choose to add religious instruction as part of their child's education, public schools must respect and accommodate that decision.

Release time religious instruction programs allow students to leave campus during part of the school day with parental permission to receive religious instruction off school property. The U.S. Supreme Court upheld such programs more than 70 years ago in Zorach v. Clauson, recognizing that accommodating religion reflects the best of the nation's traditions. However, some school districts have erected unnecessary barriers to these programs in recent years, refusing to cooperate or imposing restrictions that make participation difficult or impossible. Jeremy Dys, Senior Counsel and Chair of the Education Practice Group for First Liberty Institute, wrote that Uthmeier's opinion rightly recognizes that school districts in Florida cannot frustrate parental decisions simply because administrators prefer a different approach. Public education should complement parental authority, not compete with it.

cards.headline: Alachua County ballot set for Commission and School Board races after qualifying deadline
cards.teaser: Four Democrats will compete in an open County Commission race while incumbent School Board members face challengers in the home county of the University of Florida.
cards.body:
Florida's candidate qualifying deadline has passed and the ballot for several local Alachua County elections is set. The County Commission District 2 seat is open after incumbent Marihelen Wheeler announced she would not seek a third term. Four Democrats have qualified: Donna Bradbrook, Tina Certain, Charlie Jackson and Byran Williams. Republican Robert Woody, who formerly served as Alachua County Jail Director and was recently appointed to the Santa Fe College District Board of Trustees by Gov. Ron DeSantis, withdrew his candidacy. With only Democrats on the ballot, the Aug. 18 contest will be a Universal Primary open to all voters regardless of party and will decide the race. Certain currently serves as the District 1 School Board member and is leaving her seat to make the Commission run. Jackson, an Army veteran, unsuccessfully challenged Wheeler in the 2022 Democratic Primary but won just 27% of the vote despite outraising her. Williams, a veteran and small-business owner, has served as Mayor, Vice Mayor and a City Commissioner in High Springs. Bradbrook has raised $26,905 through the latest reporting period, including $25,000 of her own funds.

In the School Board District 3 race, incumbent Sarah Rockwell is defending her seat against challenger Gregory Pelham. Last July, Rockwell received national attention and a state reprimand for a post she made to Facebook following the death of celebrity pro wrestler Hulk Hogan. "One less MAGA in the world," Rockwell wrote. Pelham, a case manager for the Alachua County Sheriff's Office's Teen Court, is running on a slogan of less politics, more progress. With only two candidates, the District 3 winner will be decided in the August Primary. Rockwell has raised $19,610 while Pelham reports raising $7,200. District 3 includes a densely populated portion of Gainesville.

cards.headline: Florida Chamber Foundation to host workforce development summit in Tampa
cards.teaser: The June 23 summit will bring together business, education and workforce leaders to discuss strengthening Florida's talent pipeline and connecting residents to high-demand careers.
cards.body:
Card body:

The Florida Chamber Foundation will host its annual Learners to Earners Workforce Solution Summit on June 23 at the Grand Hyatt Tampa Bay. The event brings together business, education and workforce leaders to strengthen Florida's talent pipeline and connect residents to high-demand careers. Featured speakers include Byron Donalds, U.S. Assistant Secretary of Labor; Henry Mack, Education Commissioner; Stasi Kamoutsas, CareerSource Florida President and CEO; Adrienne Johnston, FloridaCommerce Secretary J. Alex Kelly; Florida Trend President and Publisher David Denor; and Arthrex Senior Director Michael Boose. The summit will focus on workforce readiness, talent development, work-based learning and strategies to meet the demands of Florida's growing economy.

The summit is organized through the Florida Chamber Foundation's Future of Work Florida Initiative and the Florida Business Alliance for Early Learning, which focuses on workforce development from early education through career placement. Topics will include early learning, career pathways, work-based learning opportunities and second-chance hiring initiatives. The event is geared toward business and industry leaders, educators, workforce professionals, economic developers and community partners working to advance the Florida 2030 Blueprint and strengthen the state's workforce pipeline. Mark Wilson, President and CEO of the Florida Chamber of Commerce and Foundation, said Florida's growing economy demands a highly skilled workforce prepared to compete in a rapidly evolving market.

hero.headline: Promise Fund seeks funding to establish breast cancer screening program in Martin County
hero.body:
Promise Fund, a South Florida nonprofit dedicated to improving breast and cervical cancer survivorship, is working to expand its screening services into Martin County. The organization currently operates four screening programs across Palm Beach and Broward counties, serving women in the three-county region who lack insurance, have inadequate coverage, or face other barriers to health care access.

Since its inception, Promise Fund has educated and reached more than 145,000 women throughout South Florida. The organization has provided screening, diagnostic services and care to more than 27,000 women and has helped 286 women diagnosed with cancer navigate their treatment options. Now the nonprofit is seeking funding to establish a similar screening program in Martin County to extend these services to additional underserved populations.

To promote access to early detection, Promise Fund is hosting two free mammography screening events next month in partnership with Florida Mobile Mammography, HealthyMe, the Health Care District of Palm Beach County, Origin Church, the Florida Department of Health and Monarch Health Services. The first event takes place July 11 starting at 8 a.m. on Indiantown Road in Jupiter, followed by a second screening on July 12 at 9 a.m. in West Palm Beach. Appointments are required to attend either event, and interested women can register by calling 877-427-7664.

Lissette Lahoz, Promise Fund's Palm Beach County navigator, emphasized the importance of the screening events. "The Promise Fund is here to make screenings accessible for everyone, especially those who might otherwise go without care," Lahoz said. She noted that early detection significantly improves treatment outcomes, saying "Early detection can make a real difference. Treatment is often easier to manage, and people are able to focus more on their health, their families, and their everyday lives." For more information about Promise Fund's services or to support the effort to establish a Martin County screening program, interested individuals and organizations can contact the nonprofit through the registration phone line.

cards.headline: Three agents join ONE Sotheby's International Realty Stuart office
cards.teaser: ONE Sotheby's International Realty has added three agents to its Stuart office.
cards.body:
THREE Sotheby's International Realty announced that three real estate agents have joined the company's Stuart office. The brokerage operates offices throughout South Florida, including locations in Martin County.

The Stuart office serves clients in the northern Treasure Coast market. ONE Sotheby's International Realty specializes in luxury residential real estate sales.

cards.headline: Florida judge rules Martin County teacher should keep his job
cards.teaser: A Florida judge has ruled that a Martin County teacher should retain employment with the school district.
cards.body:
A judge in Florida has determined that a Martin County teacher should keep his job with the school district. The ruling was issued Wednesday.

The case involved employment action taken against the teacher by Martin County school officials. The judge's decision reverses that action and allows the teacher to continue in the position.

cards.headline: Attorney challenges Florida death penalty law in Martin County murder case
cards.teaser: A defense attorney is challenging Florida's death penalty law in a Martin County murder prosecution.
cards.body:
An attorney representing a defendant in a Martin County murder case has filed a challenge to Florida's death penalty statute. The legal challenge questions the constitutionality of the state's capital punishment law.

The case is proceeding in Martin County circuit court. The challenge comes as Florida continues to use the death penalty in first-degree murder prosecutions.

cards.headline: Indian River County Ixora Park community sewage system to receive $1 million federal grant
cards.teaser: A $1 million federal grant will help fund a major sewage system upgrade in the Ixora Park community in Indian River County, affecting over 230 homes.
cards.body:
Congressman Mike Haridopolos announced Wednesday that a $1 million federal grant will help fund a $20.8 million project to retrofit the sewage system in the Ixora Park community in Indian River County. The Member Community Project Funding will affect over 230 homes that currently rely on a failing sewer system that risks contaminating environmental resources. Haridopolos said the federal support "ensures health and safety to the community by rehabilitating infrastructure for over 230 homes, while also protecting a designated federal resource, the Indian River Lagoon."

The community sits adjacent to the County South Relief Canal, which discharges into the Indian River Lagoon, one of the most diverse estuaries in the country. The project will replace aging sewer infrastructure and is designed to protect water quality by reducing discharges of nitrogen and phosphorus into the lagoon. Keith Drewett of the Clean Water Coalition of Indian River County noted that the area's high water table and heavy rainfall create conditions where water flows underground through the subsurface. Haridopolos said the benefits extend beyond environmental protection, stating the project "improves not only the quality of the water, which we all want to be out on the water, but the other part of it, you also improve the taxable value of your home."

cards.headline: Jupiter surgeon uses opioid-free recovery protocol for joint replacement patients
cards.teaser: Andrew Noble, an orthopedic surgeon at Jupiter Medical Center, is using an opioid-free protocol to help patients recover from joint replacement surgery.
cards.body:
Andrew Noble, an orthopedic surgeon at Jupiter Medical Center, is taking a different approach to post-operative pain management by helping patients recover from joint replacement surgery without opioids. He uses the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocol combined with his own proprietary method. The approach combines robotics for minimally invasive surgery, targeted numbing, and a timed schedule of non-opioid medications taken before, during, and after surgery. "Instead of chasing pain, it's a way of trying to stay ahead of pain, and have less pain afterwards with less need for opioids," Noble said.

Patient April Stubbs recovered from knee replacement surgery without opioids using Noble's approach. "I never had to touch the more serious pain medications. The opioids, never even had to take any," Stubbs said. Daniel Warren, Chief Marketing Officer at Reprieve Recovery in Jupiter, noted that patients are often unaware of the physical effects of opioid medications taken during surgical recovery and can experience withdrawals without being educated about it. Noble said the goal is straightforward: "Get patients through a surgery, better pain control, and having them with a quick recovery and satisfied results without the opioid exposure." Patients can ask their doctor if the ERAS protocol is an option for them.

cards.headline: Jupiter beach dance parties to continue at sea turtle nesting area with new lighting rules
cards.teaser: Weekend beach dance parties will continue at Jupiter's sea turtle nesting area with lighting adjustments following a meeting between town officials and stakeholders.
cards.body:
The Town of Jupiter held a meeting Wednesday afternoon at the police department to address concerns about weekend beach dance parties at a sea turtle nesting area. Local, county, and state stakeholders attended alongside representatives from Loggerhead Marinelife Center. The meeting lasted approximately an hour and a half.

Following the meeting, representatives from Happy Beach Dancing said the gathering was productive and the parties would continue with adjustments. Foreli of Happy Beach Dancing stated, "We're going to continue, just a couple of adjustments. Beautiful." The adjustments focus on reducing lighting during events to avoid disturbing nesting sea turtles, addressing calls from some community members to relocate the dancing entirely during nesting season. The group plans to return to Beach Access 55 this Saturday. Both the Town of Jupiter and Loggerhead Marinelife Center issued statements responding to the decision.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce Teen Killed in Shooting After Instagram Gun Exchange
hero.teaser: A Fort Pierce teenager was killed in a shooting that followed a planned firearm exchange arranged through Instagram.
hero.body:
A teenager in Fort Pierce was fatally shot during what police say was a planned gun exchange arranged through Instagram. The shooting occurred while the victim was riding a bicycle, marking what authorities described as an unusual incident for the area. According to Fort Pierce police, the exchange of firearms through social media leading to the fatal shooting represents a notable development in local crime patterns.

The incident has drawn attention from law enforcement as an example of how social media platforms can facilitate dangerous transactions. Police characterized the Instagram-arranged gun deal as a first of its kind in their jurisdiction, highlighting the evolving nature of criminal activity in the community. The victim, identified in available records as Maria Jesus Barajas Aguilar, was engaged in the bicycle when the shooting took place.

Investigators have been working to piece together the events that led to the deadly confrontation. Fort Pierce police continue their investigation into the circumstances surrounding the shooting, including details about who arranged the exchange and the individuals involved in the transaction. Authorities are examining how the social media platform was used to coordinate the meeting that ultimately turned fatal.

The case underscores concerns about the risks associated with arranging firearm transactions through social media channels. Police have not yet announced any arrests in connection with the shooting, and the investigation remains ongoing as detectives work to identify suspects and determine exactly what transpired during the exchange. The incident has prompted continued scrutiny of how dangerous transactions occur within local communities and the role digital platforms play in facilitating them.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Woman Maria Jesus Barajas Aguilar Dies
cards.teaser:
Maria Jesus Barajas Aguilar of Fort Pierce has died, according to an obituary posted by Haisley Funeral and Cremation Service in Fort Pierce.

Haisley Funeral a.
cards.body:
Maria Jesus Barajas Aguilar of Fort Pierce has died, according to an obituary posted by Haisley Funeral and Cremation Service in Fort Pierce.

Haisley Funeral and Cremation Service in Fort Pierce is handling arrangements for Barajas Aguilar. The funeral home posted the obituary on Wednesday.

The obituary was made available through Legacy.com, which hosts funeral home announcements. No additional information about services was provided in the announcement.

Families in Fort Pierce and surrounding areas use Haisley Funeral and Cremation Service for memorial arrangements. The funeral home serves St. Lucie County residents.

cards.headline: Family Holds Cookout and Balloon Release for Late St. Lucie County Firefighter's Birthday
cards.teaser: The family of a deceased St. Lucie County firefighter held a memorial event to honor what would have been his birthday.
cards.body:
Family members gathered to remember a St. Lucie County firefighter with a cookout and balloon release on his birthday. The event honored the late firefighter's memory.

The celebration of life event included food and a balloon release ceremony. Family members organized the gathering to mark the significant date.

The firefighter previously served St. Lucie County. His family continues to honor his service and memory through annual memorial events.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Motorcyclist Faces Super Speeder Law Penalties
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie motorcyclist will face harsher punishment under Florida's Super Speeder law.
cards.body:
A motorcyclist in Port St. Lucie is subject to enhanced penalties under the state's Super Speeder law. The law imposes stricter punishments for drivers exceeding certain speed thresholds.

The Super Speeder law triggers additional fines and consequences beyond standard speeding tickets. Motorcyclists and other drivers who reach the designated speed limit face the harsher penalties.

Port St. Lucie police enforce the Super Speeder provisions alongside regular traffic laws. The enhanced penalties apply throughout Florida when drivers meet the criteria for excessive speed.

cards.headline: Jacksonville Man Missing During Bike Trip, Last Seen in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: A Jacksonville man riding his bicycle to the Florida Keys has gone missing, with his last known location in Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
A Jacksonville man traveling by bicycle to the Florida Keys may be missing in Fort Pierce. Authorities said Fort Pierce was his last known location during the trip.

The cyclist was making the journey from Jacksonville to the Florida Keys when contact was lost. His route took him through Fort Pierce in St. Lucie County.

Anyone with information about the missing cyclist is asked to contact authorities. The man was traveling alone on his bicycle when he disappeared during the multi-day trip.

cards.headline: Planned Gun Exchange Led to Fatal Fort Pierce Bike Shooting
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police said a planned gun exchange resulted in a shooting that killed a teenager on a bicycle.
cards.body:
A teenager was killed in a Fort Pierce shooting that stemmed from a planned firearm exchange, according to police. The victim was on a bicycle when the shooting occurred.

Investigators determined the shooting was connected to an arrangement to exchange guns. The planned exchange ended in gunfire that claimed the teen's life.

Fort Pierce police continue to investigate the circumstances of the shooting. Detectives are working to identify all individuals involved in the planned gun transaction that turned deadly.

hero.headline: Father's Day weekend events planned in Sebastian and north Indian River County

cards.headline: Ixora Park sewage system in Indian River County to get $20.8 million upgrade with federal grant
cards.teaser: A $1 million federal grant will help fund a $20.8 million project to retrofit the sewage system in the Ixora Park community in Indian River County, Congressman .
cards.body:
A $1 million federal grant will help fund a $20.8 million project to retrofit the sewage system in the Ixora Park community in Indian River County, Congressman Mike Haridopolos announced at a press conference Wednesday. The Member Community Project Funding will address a failing sewer system affecting over 230 homes that risks contaminating environmental resources. The community sits adjacent to the County South Relief Canal, which discharges into the Indian River Lagoon, one of the most diverse estuaries in the country.

The project will replace aging sewer infrastructure designed to protect water quality by reducing discharges of nitrogen and phosphorus into the lagoon. Haridopolos said federal support ensures health and safety to the community while protecting the Indian River Lagoon, a designated federal resource. He noted the benefits extend beyond environmental protection, saying the infrastructure replacement improves both water quality and the taxable value of homes in the area. Keith Drewett of the Clean Water Coalition of Indian River County said the upgrade is critical because of the area's environmental conditions, explaining that the high water table and rainfall flowing underground through the subsurface make it necessary. Drewett added that the lagoon has changed dramatically over twenty years, with nobody swimming in it anymore.

cards.headline: Jupiter approves fire assessment fee for new fire rescue department starting October 1
cards.teaser: Jupiter's town council approved a fire assessment fee to help fund the town's new fire rescue department, which begins service Oct. 1.
cards.body:
Jupiter's town council has approved a fire assessment fee to help fund the town's new fire rescue department, which begins service Oct. 1. The per-property charge will cover about 8 percent of the total cost of the department. Property taxes will fund 84 percent of the department, with the remaining 8 percent collected through EMS transport fees. The assessment will replace the current county fire fee that appears on residents' tax bills.

Finance Director Scott Reynolds said the move represents significant savings for property owners. "The immediate savings for property owners, we've been talking about this for three years, starting at $25 million so right out of the gate, a $10 million savings to the residents," Reynolds said. Mayor Jim Kuretski was the lone no vote on the funding structure, raising concerns about how the assessment is calculated across different property types. Single family homes are being assessed based on total square footage including garages and porches, while townhomes and condos are not, Kuretski said. The town sent letters to 30,000 homes explaining the fee and has established an online calculator where residents can see their potential savings.

cards.headline: Jupiter beach dance parties to continue near sea turtle nesting area with new lighting rules
cards.teaser: Weekend beach dance parties will continue at Jupiter's sea turtle nesting area with lighting adjustments following a meeting with local, county and state stakeholders.
cards.body:
The Town of Jupiter held a meeting Wednesday afternoon at the police department to address concerns about weekend beach dance parties at the sea turtle nesting area. Local, county, and state stakeholders attended along with representatives from Loggerhead Marinelife Center. The meeting lasted about an hour and a half, and afterward, representatives from Happy Beach Dancing said the gathering was productive. "We're going to continue, just a couple of adjustments. Beautiful," said Foreli of Happy Beach Dancing. The group confirmed they will return to Beach Access 55 this Saturday.

The adjustments focus on reducing lighting during events to avoid disturbing nesting sea turtles. Some had called for the dancing to move away from the area entirely during nesting season, but that proposal did not prevail. Following the meeting, both the Town of Jupiter and Loggerhead Marinelife Center issued statements regarding the new decision.

cards.headline: Lake Worth Beach commission extends Benny's on the Beach lease through 2043
cards.teaser: The Lake Worth Beach City Commission unanimously approved a 10-year lease extension for Benny's on the Beach, pushing the pier restaurant's lease from January 2033 to February 2043.
cards.body:
The Lake Worth Beach City Commission unanimously approved a 10-year lease extension for Benny's on the Beach, extending the pier restaurant's lease from January 2033 to February 2043 with a 5 percent rent increase every two years. The decision followed public debate over fairness, community benefit, and whether the city should grant the extension seven years before the current agreement expires. City staff noted that Benny's had requested the maximum 30-year term allowed under city rules.

Dylan Lipton, Benny's owner, defended the extension by highlighting the restaurant's four-decade presence in Lake Worth Beach. He said Benny's employs more than 100 local residents, invests $1 million annually in maintenance, repairs, utilities, and improvements, and serves as a major tourism driver. Opposition came from residents including Jenny Powell, who questioned the timing and community benefits, and Kim Stokes, who raised concerns about unequal treatment compared to the Beach Club. Commissioner Christopher Serafinchan led advocacy for the extension, calling Benny's the city's highest-paying tenant and warning that rejecting it could bring a higher-priced replacement. Mayor Betty Resch said Benny's deserved stability. The commission approved the extension unanimously.

cards.headline: Promise Fund to offer free mammogram screenings in Jupiter and West Palm Beach in July
cards.teaser: Women in Palm Beach County will have two opportunities next month to receive free mammogram screenings through events hosted by Promise Fund.
cards.body:
Women in Palm Beach County will have two opportunities in July to receive free mammogram screenings through Promise Fund, a South Florida nonprofit focused on increasing survivorship from breast and cervical cancer. The organization will hold free Mammography Screening Days on July 11 in Jupiter and July 12 in West Palm Beach. The first event is scheduled for July 11 at 8 a.m. on Indiantown Road in Jupiter, and the second will take place July 12 at 9 a.m. in West Palm Beach. The screenings are being offered in partnership with Florida Mobile Mammography, HealthyMe, the Health Care District of Palm Beach County, Origin Church, the Florida Department of Health and Monarch Health Services.

Appointments are required for both events. Those interested can register by calling 877-427-7664. Lissette Lahoz, Promise Fund's Palm Beach County navigator, said the nonprofit is working to make screenings accessible for everyone, especially those who might otherwise go without care. "Early detection can make a real difference," Lahoz said. "Treatment is often easier to manage, and people are able to focus more on their health, their families, and their everyday lives." Promise Fund serves women throughout Palm Beach, Broward and Martin counties who are uninsured, underinsured or have limited access to health care.
